fields.foundation: The Delhi Sultanate began when the Ghurid Empire broke up after the assassination of Muhammad of Ghor in 1206. Qutb ud-Din Aibak, a Turkic slave-general who had governed the Ghurid conquests in northern India from Delhi since the victory at Tarain in 1192, assumed independent power at Lahore and founded the Mamluk or Slave Dynasty. The new state was fragile. It was contested by rival Ghurid successors such as Taj al-Din Yildiz of Ghazni and Nasir al-Din Qabacha of Multan and by resistant Rajput rulers, and its administration rested on personal loyalty, not on institutions. Consolidation went faster under Iltutmish, who seized the throne in 1211, defeated Yildiz at the third Battle of Tarain in 1216, introduced the silver tanka as the standard coin, and organised the iqta system of revenue assignments. Recognition from outside came in 1229, when the Abbasid caliph al-Mustansir Billah sent Iltutmish a formal diploma of investiture (manshur), recognising him as sultan of the lands he ruled in India. This investiture ended the sultanate's symbolic dependence on Central Asian overlords and made Delhi an independent imperial centre. Later dynasties based their own claim to authority on it.
fields.socioeconomy: The sultanate ruled one of the most populous and diverse territories of the medieval world. A Muslim ruling elite of Turkic, Afghan and Persian origin governed a predominantly Hindu agrarian population. Under the iqta system the right to collect revenue from designated territories was assigned to military officers in lieu of salary, and both the economy and the raising of armies were organised around it. Alauddin Khalji (r. 1296–1316) changed this system radically. He paid much of his army in cash, raised the land tax to half the produce in the core provinces, and imposed fixed prices enforced through state-controlled markets in Delhi for grain, cloth, horses, cattle and slaves. It was the most ambitious experiment in centralised economic management in medieval Indian history. It worked during his reign, keeping grain prices stable even in times of drought, but lapsed soon after his death in 1316 because it depended on his personal enforcement. Muhammad bin Tughlaq's token currency experiment of around 1329–1330 introduced brass and copper tokens to be accepted at the value of silver. It led to mass counterfeiting and financial chaos and had to be withdrawn. More than once the sultanate's economic innovations went beyond what its administration could sustain.
fields.military: The armies of the Delhi Sultanate were predominantly cavalry, drawing on successive waves of Turkic and Afghan martial traditions and supplemented by war elephants. Alauddin Khalji built the largest standing army the sultanate ever fielded, paid directly by the state and not through iqta assignments. The later chronicler Firishta gives it 475,000 horsemen, a figure that is certainly inflated. His general Malik Kafur led the most spectacular campaigns in the sultanate's history. He compelled the submission of the Kakatiyas at Warangal (1310), extracted enormous tribute from the Hoysala capital at Dwarasamudra and plundered the Pandya lands around Madurai (1311), so that nearly every major southern Indian power became a tributary. The sultanate's repeated success against Mongol invasions mattered as much. Alauddin's forces repelled a series of large-scale Chagatai incursions between 1297 and 1306, including the great invasion under Qutlugh Khwaja that reached the outskirts of Delhi in 1299, and northern India was spared the devastation suffered by Persia and Central Asia. The army's final failure came at the First Battle of Panipat on 21 April 1526. Ibrahim Lodi's much larger army, reportedly some 100,000 strong, was destroyed there by Babur's combination of field guns and matchlocks behind a barrier of linked carts and the flanking tulughma manoeuvre. It was among the first decisive uses of gunpowder artillery in north Indian warfare.
fields.governance: Five successive dynasties, the Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi, governed the sultanate across 320 years. Each had its own administrative emphases, but all faced the same tension between centralising royal authority and the power of the military nobility. Balban, who became sultan in 1266 after some two decades as the dominant minister under Nasir ud-Din Mahmud, confronted this tension most directly. He broke the power of the Forty (the Chihalgani), the circle of Turkic nobles who had dominated the court, introduced Persian court ceremonial to raise the ruler far above the nobility, and built an extensive network of spies. Islamic law provided the formal legal framework, administered through the courts of qazis, while Persian was the language of administration and high culture. The Transfer of capital to Daulatabad in the Deccan in 1327 was Muhammad bin Tughlaq's forced relocation of much of Delhi's elite population. It was intended to improve control of the southern provinces, but it devastated the capital, was soon reversed, and accelerated provincial rebellion. Firuz Shah Tughlaq (r. 1351–1388) later made iqtas hereditary, further strengthening the nobility. The Lodi dynasty failed to manage its Afghan nobles, who expected to be treated as peers and not as subjects. Their discontent produced the invitations to Babur, so that the sultanate was ended from within as much as from without.
fields.impact: It was chiefly through the Delhi Sultanate that Islamic legal, architectural and administrative culture took deep root in the Indian subcontinent. Persian literary and artistic traditions joined with Indian forms to produce a distinct Indo-Islamic synthesis. It can be seen in architecture from the Qutb Minar complex and Alauddin's Alai Darwaza to the Tughlaq tombs, in the poetry of Amir Khusrau, and in the emergence of the Hindavi vernacular that would later give rise to Urdu. The sultanate's successful resistance to Mongol invasion preserved northern India as a functioning centre of civilisation during the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, when much of Eurasia was devastated. Delhi became a refuge for scholars, artisans and Sufis fleeing the Mongols, and the Chishti Sufi order, led in Delhi by Nizamuddin Auliya, flourished under its rule. The Moroccan scholar Ibn Battuta's service as a qazi at Muhammad bin Tughlaq's court from 1334 reflects the sultanate's place in the wider world of Islamic scholarship and its wish to be seen as a cosmopolitan and legitimate power. After the Tughlaq decline the subcontinent broke up into regional sultanates. This permanently altered South Asian political geography and created the many separate states that the Mughal Empire would later struggle to overcome.
fields.decline: The sultanate began to break up because of the very expansion that brought it to its greatest extent. Muhammad bin Tughlaq's overextension across the south generated rebellions faster than they could be suppressed: the Madurai Sultanate broke away in 1335, the Vijayanagara Empire was founded around 1336, Bengal became independent in 1338, and the Bahmani Sultanate was established in the Deccan in 1347. Timur's sack of Delhi in December 1398 was a catastrophic physical blow. Tens of thousands were killed, by some accounts many more, many of the city's artisans were carried off to Samarkand, and the treasury was emptied. The Sayyid dynasty that followed (1414–1451) ruled as nominal vassals of the Timurids over a much-reduced territory around Delhi. The Lodi recovery under Bahlul and Sikandar was genuine but limited. It never regained the Deccan or Bengal, though Sikandar founded Agra as a new capital in 1504. Ibrahim Lodi's alienation of his own Afghan nobility proved fatal. Daulat Khan Lodi, his governor of the Punjab, and his uncle Alam Khan invited Babur to invade, and so the sultanate was destroyed by its own internal divisions as much as by external force.
fields.summary: The Delhi Sultanate created the Indo-Islamic cultural and administrative synthesis. That synthesis was carried on in South Asian civilisation through the centuries of Muslim-ruled states that followed it, above all the Mughal Empire.
fields.teaser: Five successive dynasties made the Delhi Sultanate (1206–1526) the dominant power of medieval North India. They introduced Persian administrative culture, and a syncretic Indo-Islamic civilisation grew up under them.
fields.t0: Five dynasties of Turkic and Afghan origin ruled northern India from Delhi for 320 years, from 1206 to 1526.
fields.t1: It repelled repeated Mongol invasions, and under it grew the Indo-Islamic culture of the Qutb Minar and Amir Khusrau.
fields.t2: Overreach, provincial breakaways and Timur's sack of Delhi weakened it before Babur won at Panipat in 1526.
fields.dyk: The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta served as a qazi, or judge, at the court of Muhammad bin Tughlaq in Delhi from 1334.
